answer: The namespace argument isn't an f-string: namespace='/3x3/online/{username}' is a literal string, so {username} never gets substituted with the actual value - every emit goes to a namespace nobody is ever connected to (clients connect to a concrete path like /3x3/online/alice, not the literal text /3x3/online/{username}). Fix the immediate bug with namespace=f'/3x3/online/{username}'. But per-user dynamic namespaces are an anti-pattern in Flask-SocketIO: namespaces are meant to be a small fixed set the client connects to, not one-per-user. Better: have the client connect to a single namespace, call join_room(session['username']) in your 'connect' handler, and emit with room=username instead of a dynamic namespace. Also double check the JS client is actually connecting to whatever namespace/path you use, and that session['username'] is actually set at the time this route runs (sessions aren't shared between the Socket.IO connection and unrelated HTTP requests unless cookies are configured correctly).

The most likely cause is that Employment (processed first) has no missing values, but the DataFrame's index isn't contiguous: df=df[~df.duplicated()].copy() drops rows without resetting the index, so it keeps gaps (e.g. 0,2,5,7...). mlb.fit_transform() returns a plain numpy array, and pd.DataFrame(binary_labels, ...) gets a fresh 0..n-1 RangeIndex. pd.concat([df, df_labels], axis=1) then aligns by index, not position, so mismatched indices can silently produce NaN-filled or duplicated rows once you repeat this for LanguageAdmired. Fix: call df = df.reset_index(drop=True) right after deduplication, and/or build df_labels with index=df.index explicitly. Separately, confirm Employment has no NaNs before .str.split(';') - MultiLabelBinarizer raises TypeError on a float (NaN) mixed into a column of lists, so fillna a placeholder like 'Other' before splitting, exactly as you already do for LanguageAdmired.

pivot_table's aggfunc only ever sees the values inside one group; it can't reach outside its own bucket to pull in the previous 11 months, so there's no aggfunc trick that does this in a single pivot_table call. The standard approach is two steps: first pivot to one row per month per payee with aggfunc='sum' (what you already have), then apply a trailing 12-month rolling sum on that monthly result: monthly = pd.pivot_table(df, values='value', index=pd.Grouper(freq='ME', key='date'), columns='payee', aggfunc='sum').fillna(0); rolling_12mo = monthly.rolling(window=12, min_periods=1).sum(). Rolling works cleanly here because the pivoted index is already one row per month, sorted chronologically. If you'd rather get NaN than a partial sum for months without 12 full prior periods, use min_periods=12 instead of 1.

uvw is the Windows 'windowed' counterpart of uv, analogous to python.exe vs pythonw.exe. It's the same executable as uv but built against the Windows GUI subsystem instead of the console subsystem, so launching it doesn't pop up or attach to a console window. It exists mainly so that installed GUI-script entry points (a tool with gui_scripts, e.g. a Tk/Qt app installed via uv tool install) can be launched through a uv-managed shim without a terminal window flashing up - the same reason pip/distlib ship both console and windowed launcher stubs on Windows. You generally won't invoke uvw directly yourself; it's an implementation detail of how uv creates entry-point shims on Windows, whereas uvx (uv tool run) is the one meant for everyday interactive use.

Broad question, so here's the general recipe: base your image on an NVIDIA CUDA devel image matching your host driver (e.g. nvidia/cuda:12.2.0-devel-ubuntu22.04), install build tools (build-essential, cmake, python3, python3-pip), then build llama-cpp-python with GPU support baked in via: CMAKE_ARGS='-DGGML_CUDA=on' pip install llama-cpp-python --no-cache-dir --force-reinstall (older versions used LLAMA_CUBLAS=on). Mount your GGUF model as a volume rather than baking it into the image. On the host, install nvidia-container-toolkit and configure Docker's NVIDIA runtime, then run with --gpus all (or --runtime=nvidia). Verify GPU visibility inside the container with nvidia-smi before troubleshooting llama-cpp-python itself. Your GTX 1080 (compute capability 6.1, 8GB VRAM) is supported but old enough you may need an older CUDA toolkit than the very latest if you hit 'unsupported gpu architecture' errors. Use a slim runtime-only final stage (multi-stage build) once compiled, to shrink the image.

This is PEP 695 generic syntax (Python 3.12+) combined with PEP 646 and PEP 612. T is an ordinary TypeVar: a single type parameter. *Ts is a TypeVarTuple: it captures an arbitrary-length, ordered sequence of types (like *args does for values), used for variadic generics such as array shapes or heterogeneous tuples - Ts can expand to zero or more types. **P is a ParamSpec: it captures an entire callable's parameter signature (both positional and keyword parameters) as one unit, so you can write higher-order functions/decorators that preserve the exact call signature of a wrapped callable, referencing it via Callable[P, ReturnType] or P.args/P.kwargs. All three replace the pre-3.12 pattern of declaring TypeVar('T'), TypeVarTuple('Ts'), ParamSpec('P') separately and passing them into Generic[...]. type vat[T, *Ts, **P] = ... is a generic type alias using the new 'type' statement, equivalent to the old TypeAlias pattern but with its own scoped type parameters.

Your if codesplit and codec / else structure only has two branches, so it can't express 'one present, one missing.' Build the command incrementally instead of branching on both at once: command = [ffmpeg_path, '-i', videofile]; if codesplit: command.append(codesplit); if codec: command.append(codec); command.append(outputfile). Since config.get(..., allow_no_value=True) returns either None (no value at all) or '' (empty string after '='), and both are falsy, 'if codesplit:' and 'if codec:' correctly skip either one independently while keeping the other, giving you all four combinations you listed without nested if/elif logic.

Your version calls collatz() recursively from inside its own while loop, but the recursive call number=collatz(number) passes the current, unchanged number - the even/odd branch that actually computes the next value never runs before that recursive call happens. So collatz(n) immediately calls collatz(n) again with the same n, which does the same thing, forever: it's unconditional infinite recursion regardless of the input, hence 'maximum recursion depth exceeded.' The 'correct' code avoids this because collatz() is a pure one-step transform with no loop inside it - it computes and returns the next value for a single step, and the while loop lives in the caller, calling collatz() again only after getting the previous result back. Fix your version by removing the while loop from inside the function entirely (one step per call), or alternatively drop the recursive self-call and do the transform directly, driving iteration purely from the outer while loop as the reference code does.

This looks like a version gap rather than something you're doing wrong: 'friendly'/ISO-8601 duration parsing for exclude-newer was added to uv at some point, and depending on exactly when that landed relative to 0.9.2, it may not be fully wired up for the [tool.uv] pyproject.toml key yet even though the docs describe it (vs. only the --exclude-newer CLI flag/env var supporting it). First try uv self update to get the latest release and retest - this is exactly the kind of thing that gets fixed between patch versions. If it still fails, search astral-sh/uv's GitHub issues for 'exclude-newer duration pyproject'; a report likely already exists. As a workaround meanwhile, compute an absolute RFC 3339 timestamp for 'now minus 7 days' yourself (e.g. in a small CI script) and set exclude-newer to that literal timestamp instead of a relative duration.

TypedDict doesn't support field defaults the way a dataclass or BaseModel does - bs: Optional[List[B]] = None doesn't make the key optional-to-omit, it's ignored for requiredness purposes, which is why bs still comes back as required. To mark a TypedDict key as not required, use NotRequired (PEP 655): from typing import NotRequired; class A(TypedDict): name: str; value: int; bs: NotRequired[Optional[List[B]]]. That makes bs both optional to omit and nullable, so all three of your validate_python calls should pass. If you need to support Python versions before NotRequired was added to typing, import it from typing_extensions instead.

On Android, the Tasks API's FaceLandmarker VIDEO mode has no built-in video file reader the way your desktop pipeline apparently does - you're expected to decode frames yourself and supply a timestamp for each detectForVideo() call, so there's no setting to turn that requirement off. The frame-count/prediction mismatch is most likely because you're feeding a constant interval derived from a rounded FPS (29 vs 30) rather than each frame's real presentation timestamp. Instead of computing timestamps from an assumed FPS, pull the actual per-frame timestamps from the decoder (e.g. MediaExtractor.getSampleTime() or MediaMetadataRetriever, converted to ms) and pass those exact values to detectForVideo(); that makes both frame count and timing match the container's real structure instead of an approximation, which should bring Android's output much closer to the desktop result. Exact bit-for-bit parity isn't guaranteed since the two paths use different decoders, but matching real timestamps should remove most of the divergence.

scrollIntoView() on the outer container only scrolls the container into view of the page, it doesn't scroll down inside it toward the target - and if the inner element isn't rendered yet (a virtualized/lazy list), find_element can't even locate it to scroll to. Loop instead: repeatedly scroll the container and re-check for the element each time, e.g.: for _ in range(max_tries): try: return driver.find_element(By.XPATH, element) except NoSuchElementException: driver.execute_script('arguments[0].scrollTop += arguments[0].clientHeight;', scrollableSection); time.sleep(0.3). Track the container's scrollTop before/after each step and stop (raise a timeout) once it stops increasing, meaning you've hit the bottom without finding the element. If the element already exists in the DOM but is merely outside the div's visible viewport, use arguments[0].scrollIntoView({block:'center'}) on the target element itself (once it's locatable) instead of scrolling the container blindly.

There's no single-snippet fix here - this is a systems-design problem, and plain Python (GIL-bound, dict/set-based) is a poor fit at millions-of-nodes scale regardless of how you parallelize it. Concretely: (1) BFS/DFS parallelizes at the frontier level - expand all nodes in the current frontier concurrently, merge into the next frontier, repeat; this needs process-based parallelism (multiprocessing, not threading, since traversal is CPU/dict-lookup bound), with the visited set partitioned by node-owner or synchronized via shared memory. (2) Rather than hand-rolling this, use a library with a compiled core: graph-tool or igraph for single-machine performance (far faster than networkx, much lower memory via CSR-style storage), or cuGraph if you have a GPU. (3) For out-of-core graphs, store the adjacency list as memory-mapped CSR arrays (numpy memmap) instead of a dict of lists, or push the graph into a database or a GraphFrames/Spark, Pregel-style distributed BFS if it doesn't fit one machine. Bidirectional BFS only helps for single-pair shortest path, not full reachability.

rename(mapper) with a single positional argument and no axis/columns keyword targets the index by default, not columns - that's why it errors: your row index is a plain RangeIndex, so pandas calls your lambda with a bare int, and x[0] on an int raises TypeError. Passing df.rename(columns=lambda x: f'{x[0]}_{x[1]}') instead should target columns properly, but the simplest option guaranteed to work - since it's exactly your already-working non-piped line - is to wrap it in a plain function and use pipe: def flatten_columns(df): df = df.copy(); df.columns = ['_'.join(map(str, c)) for c in df.columns]; return df. Then: df.pipe(flatten_columns). pipe doesn't require a named DataFrame method; any callable taking and returning a DataFrame works, which is exactly how you get your own 'rename_columns'-like chainable step without pandas needing to support it natively.

A likely cause: your get_client tool returns a bare Python list at the top level (return [{'id': ..., 'name': ...}]), but LangChain tool outputs get serialized into a ToolMessage that Gemini's function-calling API expects as a JSON object (struct), not a bare array - the Gemini API's function-response payload generally needs to be an object. A top-level list can end up dropped, malformed, or effectively ignored by the model even though the tool call itself succeeds. Fix: wrap the result in a dict and return that (as a dict, or a JSON string via json.dumps depending on what your tool wrapper expects), e.g. return {'clients': [{'id': ..., 'name': 'Apple'}]}, and update the docstring/return type accordingly. This is a known friction point between LangChain's google_genai integration and Gemini's stricter function-response schema compared to OpenAI's more permissive tool-message format. Also confirm you're on a recent langchain-google-genai version, since this integration's tool-message handling has changed across releases.

Standard DRF approach: don't try to make one serializer conditionally hide fields via permissions logic inside itself - pick the serializer class per request in the view. Override get_serializer_class() on your APIView/ViewSet: check request.user's role, and for the 'self vs other' case compare self.get_object() to request.user, then return one of several serializers - AdminUserSerializer (all fields), ModeratorUserSerializer (Meta.exclude the two restricted fields), SelfUserSerializer (subset + email), PublicUserSerializer (subset, no email). Example: def get_serializer_class(self): user = self.request.user; if user.is_admin: return AdminUserSerializer; if user.is_moderator: return ModeratorUserSerializer; obj = self.get_object(); return SelfUserSerializer if obj == user else PublicUserSerializer. Alternatively, use one serializer and override to_representation(self, instance) to pop fields based on self.context['request'].user - more DRY for overlapping fields, but separate serializer classes are usually clearer and easier to test since each role's contract is explicit.

Use the stdlib decimal module instead of float math: Decimal.ln() computes to whatever precision you set. Pick precision comfortably above n's size, e.g. getcontext().prec = n.bit_length() + 20, then L = Decimal(n).ln(); k = int(L) - int() truncates toward zero, which equals floor here since ln(n) >= 0 for n >= 1. Because you control precision directly (unlike float64's fixed ~15-17 digits), you can always add more guard digits, so this doesn't hit the same wall math.log(n) does. Near an integer boundary (L extremely close to an integer), recompute at higher precision and confirm it lands on the same side before trusting it. For floor(ln(n)^2), floor(ln(n)^3), floor(ln(n)^4): compute L once at high precision, then floor(L**2), floor(L**3), floor(L**4) the same way, with the same boundary re-check. mpmath is a solid alternative if you'd rather not manage decimal precision by hand.

create_task() doesn't just passively 'register' a task - it schedules the coroutine to start running at the very next opportunity the event loop gets, via loop.call_soon(), independent of whether or when anything awaits it. You created task1 then task2, so both are queued to start in that order. When await task2 suspends main and hands control to the loop, the loop drains its ready callbacks FIFO: task1 runs first, printing 'Do something with 1...' and immediately suspending at its own asyncio.sleep(1); then task2 runs, printing 'Do something with 2...' and suspending at sleep(2). Because main is awaiting task2 specifically, it stays suspended until task2 finishes at t=2, by which point task1 already finished at t=1 (its result just sat there done), so await task1 returns instantly right after. The key misconception: awaiting a task controls when you resume, not when the task starts running - it starts as soon as the loop is free to run it.

This is a long-standing upstream GtkComboBox/GtkMenu limitation: the popup is implemented with grab-based menu semantics that assume a mouse press/release pair on the same widget, which touch's synthetic event sequence doesn't reliably produce, and GTK3 no longer has a clean 'touchscreen mode' flag to fix it generically. The pragmatic workaround most people land on is to stop using GtkComboBox for touch UIs: replace it with a GtkMenuButton or plain GtkButton that opens a GtkPopover containing a GtkListBox or GtkTreeView you populate and handle selection on yourself - GtkPopover's touch handling is far more reliable than GtkMenu's since it doesn't rely on the same implicit grab-and-release model. It's more code than a drop-in fix, but it's the approach most touch-oriented GTK3 apps end up using. If migrating to GTK4 is feasible, its GtkDropDown widget handles touch natively and removes the problem outright instead of working around it.

The code you posted is cut off before the actual concat/sum, so the two most common causes of an exact 2024 doubling in this kind of notebook workflow are: (1) filtered_files accidentally contains the 2024 file twice - check for a backup/copy (e.g. 'Produce Payroll Register Data 2024 (1).xlsx', or the same year matched once as .xlsx and once as .xlsm) that also matches your regex; print(filtered_files) and confirm each year appears exactly once. (2) A classic Jupyter/VSCode notebook pitfall: re-running the 'for f in filtered_files: ... dfs.append(df)' cell without re-running the dfs = [] cell first, so the 2024 frame gets appended twice while 2025 (added later, once) isn't affected. Check len(dfs) and inspect it for duplicate frames before concatenating, and do Restart & Run All to rule out stale state before digging further - out-of-order cell execution is a very frequent source of exactly this 'one year silently doubled' symptom.
